fin_010:n1.prompt:
You are helping me pull last year's financial actuals and current runway from {{vendor}}, our accounting system, as the data foundation for next year's budget. Use my configured credentials to access {{vendor}}.

First, ask me for: (1) the exact fiscal year/period to close out (start and end dates), (2) any class, location, or department tags I want reports segmented by, and (3) where I want the output delivered (e.g., a shared doc, spreadsheet, or folder).

Then, using {{vendor}}'s reporting and API/export capabilities, do the following:
1. Generate the full-year P&L for the closing year, both consolidated and broken out by the class/location/department dimensions I specify.
2. Generate the balance sheet as of the fiscal year-end.
3. Generate the cash-flow statement for the same period.
4. Pull the general ledger and trial balance for the year in an open format (e.g., CSV) so the numbers can be independently verified or modeled later.
5. Calculate current cash runway: use the latest cash balance and the trailing 3-6 month average net burn rate (cash in minus cash out) to estimate months of runway remaining. State your calculation method and assumptions clearly.
6. Flag any anomalies, one-time items, or reclassifications in the actuals that could distort next year's modeling (e.g., large one-off expenses, revenue timing shifts).

Compile all of this into a single organized summary (or the file/doc location I specified) with clear labels for each report, the runway calculation with assumptions shown, and a short list of flagged anomalies.

When done, report back to me with: a link or location of the compiled output, the calculated runway in months, total revenue and net income for the year, and the top 3 anomalies or items I should review before building the operating plan.

fin_010:n2.prompt:
You are helping me draft next year's operating model and headcount plan for our annual budget process. Please ask me for anything you don't already have: (1) last year's actuals (P&L export or spreadsheet link), (2) current headcount roster with salaries, start dates, and department assignments, (3) known growth assumptions or revenue targets for next year, (4) any planned hires, departures, or role changes already approved, and (5) where I want the working files stored (e.g., Google Sheets, Excel/OneDrive, or a specific shared drive).

Once you have the inputs, build two linked deliverables using the spreadsheet tool I specify (default to Google Sheets if I don't have a preference):
1. An operating model that extrapolates last year's actuals into monthly and annual projections for next year, broken out by department and major expense category (payroll, tools/software, contractors, facilities, other opex), with clear formulas (not hardcoded numbers) so department leads can later stress-test assumptions.
2. A headcount plan listing every current employee plus proposed new hires, showing role, department, start month, fully-loaded annual cost, and running headcount totals by department and company-wide, tied back into the operating model's payroll line.

Flag any gaps, inconsistent data, or assumptions you had to make explicitly in a notes tab or comment thread. Do not invent numbers — if data is missing, list it as an open question rather than guessing.

When done, report back with: a link to the model and headcount plan, a short summary of total projected spend and headcount growth versus last year, and a bulleted list of open questions or assumptions that need department-lead input before the negotiation step.

fin_010:n3.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for department-lead budget negotiations as part of our annual budget & board approval process. The actual negotiation over headcount and spend trade-offs remains a human step, since it requires department leaders to resolve competing resource claims themselves. Your job is to prepare all the materials I need to run that conversation efficiently.

Please ask me for anything missing: the current draft budget model or spreadsheet (Google Sheets, Excel, or similar), the headcount plan draft, last year's actuals by department, and a list of department leads with their current requested vs. allocated budget/headcount figures.

Using these inputs, do the following:
1. Build a per-department summary showing prior-year actuals, current-year draft allocation, requested increase/decrease, and the resulting gap or surplus.
2. Flag the departments with the largest variances or most contested trade-offs (e.g., where total requests exceed total available budget), and quantify the overage.
3. Draft a one-page briefing per department lead summarizing their numbers, the key trade-off questions to raise, and 2-3 possible compromise options (e.g., phased hiring, deferred spend, reallocation from another line).
4. Prepare a master reconciliation sheet that tracks proposed compromises and outstanding open items across all departments, so I can update it live during meetings.
5. Draft a short agenda/talking-points doc for each negotiation session.

Done looks like: a complete set of per-department briefing docs, a master reconciliation tracker, and an overall summary of where the budget is over/under before any leader input is applied — all ready for me to use in live discussions with department leads.

Report back with links or file locations for each document, a summary of the biggest identified conflicts, and confirmation that this negotiation remains a human step for me to conduct directly.

fin_010:n4.prompt:
You are helping me complete the 'Circulate the budget deck to the board' step for our annual budget approval process. The deck lives in Google Slides. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the Google Slides deck link (or ask me to point you to the file in Drive), (2) the list of board member names and email addresses, (3) the target board meeting date, and (4) the deadline by which board members should submit questions or comments before the meeting.

Once you have these, please: 1) Open the deck in Google Slides and confirm it is complete (title slide, actuals recap, proposed budget model, headcount plan, key trade-offs, ask/consent request) — flag any obviously missing or placeholder slides to me rather than editing financial content yourself. 2) Set sharing permissions on the deck so board members have 'Comment' access (not edit), and confirm the link works. 3) Draft a concise email to the board list that includes: the deck link, a one-paragraph summary of the key numbers and trade-offs, the feedback deadline, and the meeting date. 4) Send the email using my configured credentials, or if you cannot send on my behalf, prepare the final draft and recipient list and tell me it's ready to send.

Done looks like: the deck is shared with correct comment-only permissions, the email is drafted (and sent, if you have that capability), and I have confirmation of who it went to and when. Report back with: the final deck link, the list of recipients, the feedback deadline stated in the email, and whether the email was sent by you or is staged for me to send.

fin_010:n5.prompt:
You are helping me manage the 'Board reviews and discusses the plan' step of our annual budget approval process. The actual board discussion of the operating plan is a live, interpersonal deliberation among fiduciaries — this remains a human step and you cannot participate in or automate it. Your job is to prepare everything needed for that discussion and then monitor for its outcome.

Please do the following:
1. Ask me for: the finalized budget model/deck location (e.g., Google Drive, Dropbox, or shared drive link), the headcount plan document, the board meeting date/time, and the list of board member names/emails if you need to send materials.
2. Compile a board packet: the operating plan summary, key assumptions, department trade-off notes from negotiations, and any open questions flagged by department leads. Organize these into a single clearly labeled document or folder.
3. Draft (but do not send) a cover email to the board with the packet attached or linked, a brief summary of key decisions/trade-offs, and a note that a vote will follow this discussion.
4. Prepare a short list of anticipated discussion questions the board may raise, based on the plan's biggest changes vs. last year's actuals, for my reference.
5. Once materials are ready, stop for human sign-off before sending anything to the board or scheduling the meeting.
6. After the meeting is expected to occur, check back with me (or check my calendar/email if you have access) to confirm whether the discussion happened and whether the board is ready to proceed to a vote. Note explicitly that you are polling/verifying an async, human-driven event, not completing it yourself.

Report back with: the compiled packet location, the drafted (unsent) email, the anticipated questions list, and confirmation that you are now waiting on the human discussion to conclude before the next step (board vote/consent) can begin.

fin_010:n6.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the board consent package that formally approves next year's operating budget, so the directors can review and sign it. This is the final step after the model, headcount plan, and department trade-offs are already settled — you are NOT approving or signing anything, only assembling and organizing the materials.

Please ask me for anything you need that isn't already available, such as: the finalized budget model/spreadsheet, the headcount plan, prior-year actuals, any notes from department-lead negotiations, our standard board consent template (if we have one), and the list of current directors with their emails.

Actions to take:
1. Compile a concise board memo summarizing the proposed budget: key totals, year-over-year changes, headcount additions, and major trade-offs or risks flagged during negotiations.
2. Draft the written consent resolution text (using our template if provided, or a standard 'unanimous written consent' format) stating that the board approves the annual operating budget as presented, leaving blank signature lines/date fields for each director.
3. Assemble a clean package (memo + supporting schedules + draft consent) in a single document or folder, organized for easy board review.
4. Prepare a short cover email draft to the board summarizing the ask and requesting their signature, without sending it.
5. Create a checklist confirming: all directors identified, materials complete, consent language accurate, and distribution method decided (e.g., e-signature tool or physical signature).

Done looks like: a complete, reviewed package ready for distribution, with the consent resolution drafted but unsigned, and a checklist confirming readiness.

Because corporate law requires actual directors to formally consent, obtaining signatures is a legal act only they can perform — this remains a human step. Do not send the package, request signatures, or mark the consent as executed. Report back with the finished package, draft cover email, and checklist, then stop for human sign-off.
